title: Twelve Times the Same Question
subtitle: One interviewer asked one question twelve times, and the audience remembered the dodge. Years earlier, a company chief answered first, and then said what mattered.

card.essence: A famous interview, a famous recall, and the three-step shape that lets you answer honestly and still say what you came to say.

intention: you'll see why an answer that is not heard is worse than a hard answer, build a three-part 'answer, bridge, message' reply, and use it to stay honest and on track when a question is difficult.
warmup: Think of a time you asked someone a direct question and did not get a direct answer. How did you feel about them afterwards?
When a question is difficult, what do you usually do first: answer, explain, or change the subject?
What is the hardest kind of question to answer in your work or studies, and why?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: When asked about the delay, he gave an evasive reply that left everyone knowing less than before.
items.meaning: evasive — avoiding giving a clear, direct answer. The verb is evade.

items.sent: The interviewer's questions were relentless: whatever the answer, the next question came at once.
items.meaning: relentless — never stopping or becoming less severe, even when you hope it will.

items.sent: She kept her composure even when the questions became personal.
items.meaning: composure — a calm state of mind that others can see, especially in a difficult moment.

items.sent: A quick, honest statement did more to reassure the public than a long defence.
items.meaning: reassure — to say or do something that makes someone feel less worried.

vocab.heading: B · Which term means…?
vocab.intro: Three terms: stay on message · dodge the question · a straight answer. Say the right one, then reveal.

items.sent: Which term means to avoid answering by changing the subject or answering a different question?
items.meaning: dodge the question — He dodged the question twice before the audience noticed.

items.sent: Which term means a clear, direct and honest reply?
items.meaning: a straight answer — All I want is a straight answer: yes or no?

items.sent: Which term means to keep returning to your main point, whatever you are asked?
items.meaning: stay on message — The spokesperson stayed on message throughout the interview. Often used critically, when the repetition is too obvious.

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.sent: ___ a statement  ·  ___ a warning  ·  ___ a recall
items.meaning: issue — to publish or announce something officially: a statement, a warning, a recall, an apology.

items.sent: ___ a promise  ·  ___ your word  ·  ___ a secret
items.meaning: keep — keep a promise, keep your word, keep a secret.

items.sent: come under ___  ·  crack under ___  ·  work well under ___
items.meaning: pressure — a feeling of being forced to act, speak or decide quickly in a difficult situation.

vocab_use: Tell me about a public figure or a company that gave a straight answer when it was difficult. What did it do to reassure people?
Describe a time you saw someone dodge the question. How could you tell?
Who do you know who keeps their composure under pressure? What do they do differently?

story.heading: Part 1 — One question, asked again
paras: On 13 May 1997, a former British Home Secretary named Michael Howard sat down for a live interview on the BBC programme Newsnight. He had left the Home Office two weeks earlier. Two years before that, as Home Secretary, he had been in a dispute with the head of the Prison Service, Derek Lewis, about the possible dismissal of a prison governor.

The interviewer, Jeremy Paxman, put one question: did you threaten to overrule him? Howard did not say yes or no. He answered with sentences about what he had and had not done, among them that he had not overruled Mr Lewis, which was a slightly different thing.
Paxman asked again. And again. Most counts say the same question was asked twelve times, though some count fourteen, depending on how the first questions are measured.
checks: Who was being interviewed, and what position had he held?
How many times was it asked?
answers: Michael Howard, a former British Home Secretary.
Did you threaten to overrule him? (him being the head of the Prison Service).
About twelve times; some people count fourteen.
story.discuss: Howard's answer was technically true: he had not overruled the head of the Prison Service. Why did that not satisfy the audience?

story.heading: Part 2 — What the audience heard
paras: People remember the interview today, but few remember the dispute. What stayed with them was the pattern: a clear question, a reply that sounded as if it came from a different one, and then the same question again. For many viewers, the answer to the question mattered less than the evasion itself.

Years later, Howard joked about it. In 2014, on the last Newsnight that Paxman presented, he told the interviewer that he had not threatened to overrule, and invited him to ask another eleven times. Paxman himself admitted that part of the reason he repeated the question was that the next item in the programme was not ready.

Whether Howard did or did not threaten anyone is not the point of this lesson. The point is what listeners do with an answer that does not answer: they stop hearing the content and start hearing the avoidance.
checks: What do people remember about the interview today?
What did Howard say to Paxman in 2014?
What does Paxman say was partly the reason for repeating the question?
answers: The repetition and the sense of an evasive answer, more than the details of the dispute.
That he had not threatened to overrule, and that Paxman could feel free to ask another eleven times.
The next item in the programme was not ready, so he needed to fill time.
story.discuss: A listener who spots an evasion stops trusting the rest of what you say. Can you remember a time when this happened to you? What did the speaker do next?

story.heading: Part 3 — Seven deaths and a decision
paras: In September 1982, seven people in the Chicago area died after taking Tylenol capsules that someone had filled with cyanide. The person responsible was never found. The product was made by Johnson & Johnson, whose chairman at the time was James Burke.

Burke put himself in front of the cameras. The company and the authorities told the public not to take Tylenol. Within days, Johnson & Johnson withdrew about thirty-one million bottles from shelves across the country, at a cost of around a hundred million dollars, even though the poisoning seemed to affect only some capsules in the Chicago area.

In effect, he answered the question the public was asking, which was whether Tylenol was safe, and he answered it directly: not now. Then he moved to the message he wanted people to hear, which was that the company's first concern was public safety. Some writers say the legend is tidier than events were, but the shape of his replies remains the standard example of the answer first, then the message.
checks: What had happened to the Tylenol capsules in 1982?
What was the order of Burke's replies?
answers: Someone had put cyanide in some capsules, and seven people died.
It withdrew about thirty-one million bottles nationwide, at a cost of around a hundred million dollars.
He answered the question honestly first, then moved to the message that public safety came first.
story.discuss: Burke's answer was uncomfortable for the company, because it meant a big loss. Why can an honest, costly answer build trust faster than a safe one?

tool_tab.lead: Media trainers teach a technique called bridging: answer the question, then link to the point you most want to make. Used well, it keeps you honest and on track. Used badly, it is the dodge from Part 1. The tool below keeps the three moves in order so that the answer always comes first.
how: Answer the question you were asked, in one sentence. If the answer is yes, say yes. If it is no, say no. If you do not know, say that: I don't know yet. We should have the figures on Thursday.
Bridge with one short linking phrase: What matters more is…, The important thing for our customers is…, Let me put that in context…
Message: say the one thing you most want the listener to take away. One point, in one sentence.
Stop and let the listener respond. If the same question comes again, give the same honest answer in fewer words, then bridge to a different aspect of the message.

sort.intro: These sentences come from replies to difficult questions. What job does each one do? Choose, then check.

items.text: Yes, the project is about three weeks late.
items.why: a direct reply to the question, with no softening.

items.text: I don't think that's the right question to be asking.
items.why: it rejects the question instead of answering it, and the listener hears the avoidance.

items.text: That's an important point, and what I would add is this.
items.why: it acknowledges the question and moves to a new point; it only works after an answer.

items.text: Every customer affected will be refunded in full this month.
items.why: the one thing the speaker most wants remembered.

items.text: No. The earlier forecast was wrong.
items.why: a short, honest reply, even though it is uncomfortable.

items.text: Well, there are many ways of looking at it.
items.why: it sounds like an answer but contains none.

items.text: Let me put that in context.
items.why: a short phrase that moves from the answer to the message.

items.text: Our first priority is that nobody is put at risk.
I can't say yet — we won't have the figures until Thursday.
items.why: an honest answer when you do not know, with the date it will be known.

items.text: As I have already said, I'm not going to get into that.
items.why: it refuses without explaining why, which sounds as though something is being hidden.

breaks: Yes-or-no questions about something serious. If the listener has been harmed, or has asked a plain question of fact, the answer is all they want. Bridge later, if at all.
Listeners who are upset. Before the message, they need to hear that you understand. A bridge that arrives too quickly sounds cold: I'm sorry. I understand why you're angry.
When the bridge is the only thing you say. A message repeated in every reply, whatever the question, is the dodge from Part 1. The listener hears the avoidance, not the point.
discuss: Where is the line between a bridge and a dodge? How would a listener know?
When did you last answer a difficult question honestly and then regret it? What would you do differently now?

grammar.name: Concession, then focus
grammar.lead: A bridge is a small piece of grammar: it admits one thing and moves attention to another. The structures below let you do that without sounding evasive.
notes: Concession clauses: Although it is true that…, the more important point is… / While we did miss the deadline, what matters now is… The first clause admits; the second clause moves.
Wh-clefts to focus attention: What matters most is… / What I would add is… / All I can say is… The first part announces a point, and is delivers it.
Content clauses with that: The thing to bear in mind is that… / The important point is that… / What we know is that… After is, a that-clause names the message.

exercises.heading: Build the bridge
exercises.intro: Use each word from the box once: although · what · which · that.
items: 1. ___ it is true that the project is late, the budget is safe.
2. ___ matters most to our customers is a clear date.
3. The point to bear in mind is ___ nobody has been harmed.
4. Delivery slipped by three weeks, ___ is why we are offering refunds.

exercises.heading: Which reply answers first?
exercises.intro: In each pair, choose the reply that gives the answer before anything else.
items:
1. Did the delivery arrive on time?
(a) Well, there were weather problems in the north, and the carrier changed hands last month, and as it happens…
(b) No, it was two days late. The carrier had weather problems, and we have a new schedule from Monday.

2. Will you refund me?
(a) Yes. You will have the money within five days, and I'm sorry for the delay.
(b) I understand how frustrating this must be, and we take every complaint seriously, and…

3. Is the product safe?
(a) Safety is our first priority and we always follow strict procedures, and…
(b) Not at the moment. We have stopped sales until the checks are finished.

4. Do you know who is responsible?
(a) I don't know yet, and I won't guess. We will tell you as soon as we do.
(b) That's a very good question, and what I would say is that we are looking into every possibility.
answers: 1. (b) — the answer comes first, then the reason.
2. (a) — it begins with the answer and adds an apology.
3. (b) — a direct answer, even though it is uncomfortable.
4. (a) — it admits what is not known and gives a time.

grammar.closing: Now think of a difficult question you were asked this month and answer it again, with the answer first, using one of the openers from this page.

speak.intro: Plan the three moves, then speak. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk.
speak.useful: “The short answer is…” · “What matters more is…” · “Let me put that in context…” · “The important thing is that…” · “I don't know yet, but…”

tasks.label: Task 1 — The question asked three times
paras: Choose one of these questions: Why did the price go up so much? / Why were you not ready? / Why should we trust you? You will be asked it three times. Give the same honest answer each time, shorter each time, and bridge to a different point each time.

tasks.label: Task 2 — Hard questions
paras: Pick two of these and answer each in twenty seconds: Is it true that you cut corners to finish on time? / Do you accept that the first plan was a mistake? / What would you say to someone who lost money because of this? Answer, bridge, message. Then say which of your two replies sounded more honest and why.

tasks.label: Task 3 — The story in sixty seconds
paras: Tell the story of the Newsnight interview and the Tylenol recall in sixty seconds, starting with the message: what is the difference between the two?

final: Is it ever right to say 'I am not going to answer that'? How would you say it so that the listener keeps trusting you?
Burke paid a hundred million dollars for honesty. What does a speaker gain by being honest, when the cost is very high?
Where is the line between a bridge and a dodge? Give an example of a reply on each side of the line.
From memory: explain answer, bridge and message in four sentences, using the short answer is, what matters more is, dodge the question and a straight answer.

practice.intro: One page of difficult questions for using Answer, Bridge, Message again and again. Pick a question, take ten seconds to decide your honest answer and your one message, and reply in thirty seconds or less.
steps: Ten seconds: what is the true answer, in one sentence? What is the one message that matters most to this listener?
Thirty seconds: the answer first, then one linking phrase, then the message.
Stop and wait. If the same question comes back, give a shorter answer.

groups.title: A customer is unhappy
groups.intro: They want a straight answer and some respect.
questions: Why has my order not arrived?
Why does it cost so much more than last year?
Why can't I speak to a manager?
Will I get my money back?
How do I know this won't happen again?

groups.title: A manager is concerned
groups.intro: The listener has authority and little time.
questions: Why are we behind schedule?
Did you know about this problem a month ago?
Whose fault is it?
Will we still hit the target?
Why should I trust this forecast when the last one was wrong?

groups.title: A public question
groups.intro: The audience is listening for evasion.
questions: Do you accept that mistakes were made?
Why did it take so long to respond?
Are people at risk?
What do you say to those who feel let down?
Will anyone lose their job over this?

groups.title: An interview
groups.intro: A direct question about a weakness.
questions: Why did you leave your last job?
What is your biggest weakness?
Tell me about a time you failed.
Why is there a gap in your CV?
Why do you think you are ready for this role?

groups.title: A colleague or friend
groups.intro: It is personal, and the honest answer is uncomfortable.
questions: Did you read what I sent you?
Why didn't you tell me earlier?
Do you think I made the wrong decision?
Are you angry with me?
Can you help me with this, even though you're busy?

models.q: Why has my order not arrived?
parts: Answer
Because it was dispatched two days late, and that was our mistake.
Bridge
What matters now is getting it to you.
Message
It will arrive by Thursday, and if it does not, we will refund the full amount.

models.q: Did you know about this problem a month ago?
parts: Answer
Yes, we knew about a smaller version of it.
Bridge
What I want to be clear about is what we did next.
Message
We tested the fix, and it did not work well enough. That is why we are changing the process now.

models.q: Why is your price higher than last year?
parts: Answer
Our costs rose by about twelve per cent, and we have passed on most of it.
Bridge
The important thing for you is what that buys.
Message
The price includes a longer warranty, and the average repair under it costs more than the increase.

models.q: Why did you leave your last job?
parts: Answer
The company was cutting my department, and I decided to leave before the cuts.
Bridge
That gave me time to think about what I really want.
Message
What I want is a role where I can build things, and that is why I applied here.

models.q: Do you accept that mistakes were made?
parts: Answer
Yes. We were slow to act, and that was wrong.
Bridge
What matters most now is what we do about it.
Message
Every affected family will be contacted this week, and an independent review will start on Monday.

models.q: Will we still hit the target?
parts: Answer
Not at the current rate, no.
Bridge
Here is what would change that.
Message
If we move two people to the final stage, we reach it in six weeks.

harder: Shorter: answer in ten seconds, bridge in one sentence.
Again: your partner asks the same question three times. Give the same honest answer each time, shorter each time, and bridge to a different point.
Hostile: your partner interrupts after your answer with That's not an answer! Reply calmly, without raising your voice or repeating yourself word for word.
Opposite: answer the same question again with the opposite answer. Where would your message come from?
Upset listener: say one sentence that shows you understand how the listener feels before you bridge.
